content: Children often experience significant fear and anxiety when undergoing dental treatment, which can result in behavioral challenges for the dentist. These challenges can hinder the successful completion of dental procedures. Sedation is a commonly used approach to alleviate anxiety and manage behavior in pediatric dental patients. However, it is essential to identify which sedation agents, dosages, and regimens are most effective based on existing research. This review represents the second update of a Cochrane Review originally published in 2005 and updated in 2012. The primary objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and comparative effectiveness of various conscious sedation agents and dosages for managing behavior in children undergoing dental treatment. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Oral Health Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase, up to February 22, 2018. Additionally, ongoing trials were identified through the US National Institutes of Health Ongoing Trials Register (ClinicalTrials.gov) and the World Health Organization International Clinical Trials Registry Platform. No restrictions were applied regarding language or publication date during the search. The inclusion criteria for this review were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that compared two or more sedation drugs, techniques, or placebos in children up to 16 years of age, with the sedation administered by a dentist or a member of the dental team. Cross-over trials were excluded from the analysis. Data extraction and analysis were performed independently by two review authors. They collected detailed information on study methods, participant characteristics, interventions, outcome measures, and results. When trial reports were unclear or incomplete, the authors contacted the original investigators for clarification. The included studies were assessed for risk of bias, and statistical analyses were conducted following Cochrane guidelines. A total of 50 studies involving 3,704 participants were included in the review. Of these, 40 studies (81%) were deemed to have a high risk of bias, nine studies (18%) had an unclear risk of bias, and only one study was assessed as having a low risk of bias. Across the studies, 34 different sedative agents were evaluated, either alone or in combination with inhalational nitrous oxide. The dosages, modes of administration, and timing of administration varied significantly among the studies. The studies were categorized into placebo-controlled trials, dosage comparisons, and head-to-head comparisons of different sedatives. Meta-analysis was only feasible for studies comparing oral midazolam to placebo in terms of the primary outcome, which was cooperative behavior during dental treatment. Moderate-certainty evidence from six small studies, which were clinically heterogeneous and had a high or unclear risk of bias, indicated that oral midazolam at doses ranging from 0.25 mg/kg to 1 mg/kg was associated with significantly improved cooperative behavior compared to placebo. The standardized mean difference (SMD) favored midazolam (SMD 1.96, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.59 to 2.33, P < 0.0001, I² = 90%; 6 studies; 202 participants). However, conclusions regarding secondary outcomes could not be drawn due to inconsistent or insufficient reporting. In conclusion, there is moderate-certainty evidence supporting the effectiveness of oral midazolam as a sedative agent for children undergoing dental treatment. However, further well-designed and rigorously reported clinical trials are necessary to evaluate other potential sedation agents. Future research should focus on comparing experimental sedation regimens with oral midazolam or inhaled nitrous oxide to establish their relative efficacy.
